intro: Discover the perfect introduction to Bhutan with our Fly In Fly Out - 4 Nights / 5 Days itinerary. Thoughtfully designed for travellers who want to experience Bhutan's rich culture, peaceful landscapes and iconic landmarks in a comfortable timeframe, this journey combines the country's two most popular destinations—Thimphu, the vibrant capital, and Paro, home to the legendary Tiger's Nest Monastery.

From ancient monasteries and traditional architecture to scenic mountain valleys and authentic Bhutanese hospitality, every day offers a meaningful glimpse into the Kingdom of Bhutan. Whether you're visiting for the first time, travelling with family, planning a honeymoon or seeking a peaceful Himalayan escape, this itinerary provides a well-balanced travel experience with comfortable driving distances and carefully planned sightseeing.
highlights: Experience Bhutan's two most iconic destinations – Thimphu and Paro.
Discover Bhutan's culture through monasteries, dzongs and traditional architecture.
Visit Buddha Dordenma, Tashichho Dzong, Rinpung Dzong and the National Museum.
Hike to the legendary Tiger's Nest Monastery (Taktsang).
Enjoy scenic Himalayan landscapes with comfortable driving distances.

itinerary.title: Arrival at Paro (2,250m)
itinerary.desc: Upon your arrival at Paro International Airport, our representative will warmly welcome you and assist with your transfer to the hotel. After check-in and some time to relax, begin exploring the beautiful Paro Valley. Visit Rinpung Dzong, one of Bhutan's most important fortress monasteries, admired for its traditional Bhutanese architecture and rich Buddhist heritage. Walk across the historic wooden cantilever bridge before continuing to Kyichu Lhakhang, one of the oldest and most sacred temples in Bhutan. Later, visit Drukgyel Dzong, a historic fortress built in 1649 to commemorate Bhutan's victory over Tibetan invaders. The site also offers beautiful views of Mount Jomolhari (7,326m), one of Bhutan's highest Himalayan peaks. Spend the evening exploring Paro town, browsing local handicraft shops, visiting cafés, or simply enjoying the peaceful surroundings before your overnight stay in Paro.

itinerary.title: Tiger's Nest Monastery hike and Drive from Paro to Thimphu (2,350m)
itinerary.meta: 54 km · Approx. 2 Hours
itinerary.desc: After breakfast, begin the hike to Paro Taktsang, popularly known as Tiger's Nest Monastery. Perched on a cliff about 900 metres above Paro Valley, it is Bhutan's most recognised monastery and one of the country's most important Buddhist pilgrimage sites. According to Buddhist tradition, Guru Rinpoche meditated here in the 8th century after arriving on the back of a flying tigress. The hike offers spectacular views of Paro Valley while providing an opportunity to experience Bhutan's spiritual heritage. After descending, enjoy lunch before driving to Thimphu, the capital city of Bhutan. Spend the evening exploring Thimphu town, browsing local handicraft shops, visiting cafés, or enjoying the relaxed atmosphere before your overnight stay in Thimphu.

itinerary.title: Sightseeing in Thimphu
itinerary.desc: After breakfast, enjoy a full day exploring Bhutan's capital city. Visit the National Memorial Chorten, an important Buddhist monument where local residents gather daily for prayers. Continue to Buddha Dordenma at Buddha Point, one of the world's largest seated Buddha statues, offering panoramic views of Thimphu Valley. Later, visit the Motithang Takin Preserve, home to Bhutan's national animal. Continue your sightseeing with visits to the National Library, the National Institute of Traditional Medicine, the Textile Museum, the Traditional Handmade Paper Factory and the Handicrafts Emporium to learn more about Bhutan's rich cultural heritage and traditional craftsmanship. Conclude the day's sightseeing with a visit to Tashichho Dzong, the administrative and religious centre of Bhutan, before returning to your hotel for an overnight stay in Thimphu.

itinerary.title: Excursion to Punakha via Dochula Pass (3,050m)
itinerary.meta: 75 km One Way · Approx. 2.5 Hours
itinerary.desc: After breakfast, drive to Punakha via Dochula Pass, one of Bhutan's most scenic mountain passes. Visit the famous 108 Druk Wangyal Chortens before continuing your journey through the picturesque Himalayan landscape. Continue to Punakha Dzong, built in 1637 at the confluence of the Pho Chhu and Mo Chhu rivers. It is one of Bhutan's most significant religious and historical landmarks. After lunch, enjoy a pleasant walk through the countryside to Chimi Lhakhang, also known as the Fertility Temple, dedicated to Lama Drukpa Kunley, widely known as the Divine Madman. Later, drive back to Thimphu and spend the evening at leisure before your overnight stay in Thimphu.

itinerary.desc: After breakfast, check out from your hotel and drive to Paro International Airport for your onward flight . Your Fly In Fly Out Bhutan journey concludes today. Crafted with care by La Bhutanz Tours.

Explore traditional villages, ancient monasteries and the beautiful valleys that make Bumthang one of the kingdom's most treasured destinations. Later, visit Mebar Tsho (Burning Lake), one of Bhutan's most sacred pilgrimage sites, and enjoy interactions with local communities and traditional weaving households. Overnight at Bumthang.

itinerary.title: Excursion to Ura Valley (3,100m)
itinerary.meta: Approx. 54 km One Way · Approx. 3 Hours
itinerary.desc: Enjoy a scenic excursion to Ura Valley, one of Bhutan's highest and most picturesque villages. Travel through beautiful landscapes and visit Ura Monastery while experiencing the traditional lifestyle and architecture of the region. Spend time strolling through the peaceful village and enjoy the serene atmosphere of Central Bhutan before returning to Bumthang. Later, visit local farms and traditional establishments producing apple juice, cider and cheese. Overnight at Bumthang.

itinerary.title: Bumthang (2,600m)
itinerary.meta: Transfer to Punakha (1,310m) · Approx. 212 km · Approx. 8 Hours
itinerary.desc: Begin your return journey towards Western Bhutan, retracing the scenic mountain route through Trongsa and Pele La Pass. Enjoy leisurely stops along the way, taking in Bhutan's ever-changing landscapes and peaceful countryside. Upon arrival in Punakha, spend the remainder of the day relaxing amidst the valley's pleasant climate and tranquil surroundings. Overnight at Punakha.

itinerary.title: Punakha (1,310m)
itinerary.meta: Transfer to Paro (2,280m) · Approx. 140 km · Approx. 5 Hours
itinerary.desc: Continue your journey towards the beautiful valley of Paro. Enroute, visit Lamperi and the Royal Botanical Park, home to a rich diversity of Himalayan flora and fauna. Upon arrival in Paro, explore the National Museum housed within Ta Dzong and visit the historic Rinpung Dzong, an architectural masterpiece overlooking the valley. Spend the evening at leisure exploring Paro town. Overnight at Paro.

itinerary.title: Explore Paro & Excursion to Tiger's Nest Monastery (3,120m)
itinerary.desc: Embark on one of Bhutan's most memorable experiences with an excursion to the iconic Tiger's Nest Monastery. Perched dramatically on a cliff nearly 900 meters above the valley floor, Taktsang Monastery is Bhutan's most revered pilgrimage site and one of the kingdom's most recognisable landmarks. Later, visit the historic Drukgyel Dzong and Kyichu Lhakhang, one of Bhutan's oldest and most sacred temples, before spending time exploring the beautiful surroundings of Paro Valley. Overnight at Paro.

itinerary.title: Excursion to Chele La Pass (3,810m)
itinerary.meta: Approx. 35 km One Way · Approx. 2 Hours
itinerary.desc: Enjoy a scenic drive to Chele La Pass, the highest motorable road in Bhutan. The route passes through beautiful forests of pine, spruce and rhododendron before opening to spectacular panoramic views of the Himalayan mountain ranges and pristine valleys below. On clear days, enjoy breathtaking views of Mount Jomolhari (7,326m), one of Bhutan's most sacred peaks, along with several surrounding Himalayan summits. Spend time amidst fluttering prayer flags, crisp mountain air and the peaceful alpine surroundings before returning to Paro. The remainder of the day may be spent relaxing, exploring Paro town, shopping for local handicrafts or simply enjoying your final evening in the Kingdom of Bhutan. Overnight at Paro.

itinerary.title: Departure from Paro
itinerary.desc: Bid farewell to the Kingdom of Bhutan as you transfer to Paro International Airport for your onward journey. As your Explore Bhutan journey comes to an end, take with you unforgettable memories of sacred monasteries, spectacular mountain landscapes, traditional villages and meaningful cultural experiences. From the peaceful valleys of Punakha and Bumthang to the iconic landmarks of Paro, this journey offers a deeper understanding of Bhutan's timeless beauty and enduring traditions.

faqs.q: Is 10 Nights / 11 Days enough to explore Bhutan properly?
faqs.a: Yes. This itinerary offers a well-paced journey covering both Western and Central Bhutan, including Thimphu, Punakha, Bumthang and Paro, allowing travellers to experience Bhutan beyond the usual highlights.

faqs.q: Why does this itinerary include three nights in Bumthang?
faqs.a: Bumthang is regarded as the spiritual heartland of Bhutan and is home to some of the kingdom's oldest monasteries, sacred temples and traditional villages. The extended stay allows for a deeper and more immersive experience.

faqs.q: Is the drive to Bumthang very long?
faqs.a: The journey to Bumthang involves scenic mountain drives through Central Bhutan. While the drive is longer than Western Bhutan routes, the landscapes, mountain passes and cultural experiences make it one of Bhutan's most rewarding journeys.

faqs.q: Is the Tiger's Nest hike suitable for all travellers?
faqs.a: The hike requires a moderate level of fitness and can be completed at a comfortable pace. Travellers who prefer not to undertake the full hike may visit the viewpoint café or enjoy leisure time in Paro.

faqs.q: What is the best time to undertake this journey?
faqs.a: Spring (March to May) and Autumn (September to November) are considered the best seasons, offering pleasant weather, clear Himalayan views and vibrant landscapes. However, the itinerary can be enjoyed throughout much of the year.

faqs.q: Is this itinerary suitable for senior travellers?
faqs.a: Yes. The journey follows a comfortable pace with multiple-night stays and avoids excessively rushed travel, making it suitable for senior travellers seeking a deeper Bhutan experience.

faqs.q: Can this itinerary be customised?
faqs.a: Absolutely. Additional experiences such as wellness activities, village experiences, festivals, photography opportunities and luxury stays can be incorporated according to your travel preferences.

faqs.q: What makes this itinerary different from shorter Bhutan tours?
faqs.a: Unlike shorter itineraries that focus mainly on Paro, Thimphu and Punakha, this journey extends into Central Bhutan and offers a deeper understanding of Bhutan's spiritual heritage, traditional lifestyles and diverse landscapes.

faqs.q: Is this journey suitable for families and couples?
faqs.a: Yes. This itinerary is ideal for families, couples and travellers seeking a meaningful Himalayan journey with a balanced combination of culture, spirituality, nature and relaxation.

Bhutan is one of the few destinations in the Himalayas where photography extends far beyond landscapes. From ancient monasteries perched on cliffs and pristine valleys filled with prayer flags to remote eastern villages preserving centuries-old traditions, every region offers unique visual stories waiting to be captured.

This 12 Nights / 13 Days Photography Journey has been thoughtfully designed for travellers, photography enthusiasts and visual storytellers seeking a deeper exploration of Bhutan. The journey gradually unfolds from the western valleys of Paro and Thimphu to the lesser-visited regions of Eastern Bhutan, offering opportunities to photograph dramatic mountain scenery, traditional architecture, local communities, monasteries, village life, festivals (seasonal), wildlife and everyday moments that define Bhutan's unique identity.

itinerary.title: Arrive at Paro International Airport
itinerary.meta: Explore Paro Valley (2,280m)
itinerary.desc: As your flight approaches Paro, enjoy spectacular aerial views of the Eastern Himalayas, including the sacred peaks of Mount Jomolhari and Jichu Drake. Upon arrival at Paro International Airport, you will be warmly welcomed by your Bhutanese guide. After completing arrival formalities and discussing your photography journey, spend the afternoon exploring Paro Valley. Depending on arrival time, enjoy introductory photography sessions around traditional Bhutanese architecture, local settlements and the beautiful Paro landscape. Overnight at Paro.

itinerary.title: Explore Paro Valley (2,280m)
itinerary.desc: After breakfast, visit the historic ruins of Drukgyel Dzong, once a strategic fortress that commemorates Bhutan's victory over Tibetan invasions. On clear days, enjoy magnificent views of Mount Jomolhari (7,329m), one of Bhutan's most sacred mountains. Continue to Kyichu Lhakhang, one of Bhutan's oldest and holiest temples, built in the 7th century by Tibetan King Songtsen Gampo. Later, visit the National Museum, which houses an impressive collection of Bhutanese cultural artefacts and offers excellent opportunities for architectural photography. Conclude the day with a visit to Rinpung Dzong and a leisurely walk through Paro town, capturing traditional Bhutanese life and the iconic wooden cantilever bridge. Overnight at Paro.

itinerary.title: Excursion to Tiger's Nest Monastery (Taktsang Monastery) (3,120m)
itinerary.desc: Today embark on one of Bhutan's most rewarding experiences as you hike to the iconic Tiger's Nest Monastery. Perched dramatically on a cliff approximately 900 metres above the Paro Valley, this sacred monastery is one of Bhutan's most revered pilgrimage sites. According to legend, Guru Rinpoche arrived here on the back of a flying tigress and meditated in a cave, giving the monastery its name. The hike offers exceptional opportunities for landscape and monastery photography. Enjoy a picnic lunch at the Taktsang Cafeteria overlooking the monastery and surrounding valley. The round hike generally takes around 4–5 hours. Overnight at Paro.

itinerary.title: Excursion to Haa Valley via Chele La Pass (3,822m)
itinerary.desc: Rise early for a scenic excursion to the beautiful Haa Valley via Chele La Pass, Bhutan's highest motorable pass. Drive through dense forests of pine and rhododendron while enjoying magnificent panoramic views of the Himalayan mountain ranges. Chele La offers exceptional sunrise and landscape photography opportunities. Continue towards the peaceful Haa Valley, known for its pristine landscapes, traditional villages and untouched Bhutanese charm. Enjoy a picnic lunch before returning to Paro. En route, visit the peaceful Chele La Nunnery and capture the stunning mountain scenery. Overnight at Paro.

itinerary.title: Paro (2,280m)
itinerary.meta: Transfer to Thimphu (2,334m) · Approx. 55 km · Approx. 1.5 Hours
itinerary.desc: After breakfast, drive to Bhutan's capital city, Thimphu. En route, visit Simtokha Dzong, one of the oldest fortresses in Bhutan, built in 1629 and presently home to one of the country's premier monastic institutions. Upon arrival in Thimphu, visit the impressive Tashichho Dzong, which houses the King's office, government ministries and the central monastic body. Later, visit the Memorial Chorten, built in memory of the Third King of Bhutan. Continue to Sangaygang View Point for panoramic views of Thimphu Valley and visit the Zilukha Nunnery. You may also explore the Traditional Arts and Crafts School and local handicraft centres, offering excellent opportunities for cultural and documentary photography. Overnight at Thimphu.

itinerary.title: Thimphu (2,334m)
itinerary.meta: Transfer to Gangtey Valley (3,000m) · Approx. 135 km · Approx. 5–6 Hours
itinerary.desc: After breakfast, begin your scenic drive towards the beautiful Gangtey Valley via Dochula Pass (3,150m). Stop at Dochula Pass to photograph the iconic 108 Druk Wangyal Chortens and, weather permitting, enjoy spectacular views of the snow-capped Eastern Himalayan mountain ranges. Continue your journey through changing landscapes as the road descends into subtropical valleys before climbing towards the pristine Phobjikha Valley. Gangtey Valley is renowned for its wide glacial landscapes, traditional villages and, during winter months, the endangered Black-Necked Cranes. Enjoy the peaceful surroundings and capture the valley's unique natural beauty. Overnight at Gangtey.

itinerary.title: Gangtey Valley (3,000m)
itinerary.meta: Transfer to Bumthang (2,600m) · Approx. 180 km · Approx. 6–7 Hours
itinerary.desc: This morning, continue your journey towards Bumthang via Trongsa. Enroute, visit Chendebji Chorten, an important stupa built in the 18th century and inspired by Nepal's Swayambhunath Stupa. Proceed to visit the magnificent Trongsa Dzong, one of Bhutan's most historically significant fortresses and the ancestral home of Bhutan's Royal Family. Continue your drive across scenic mountain passes and forested landscapes before arriving in Bumthang, often regarded as the cultural and spiritual heartland of Bhutan. Later, visit Jakar Dzong, Jambay Lhakhang and local handicraft centres, offering wonderful opportunities to photograph Bhutan's traditional architecture and cultural heritage. Overnight at Bumthang.

itinerary.title: Explore Bumthang Valley (2,600m)
itinerary.desc: After breakfast, enjoy a full day exploring the cultural treasures of Bumthang Valley. Visit Chakhar Lhakhang, the site associated with the ancient palace of Sindhu Raja, followed by Kurjey Lhakhang, one of Bhutan's most sacred monasteries. Continue to Tamshing Lhakhang, one of the kingdom's most important Nyingma monasteries, known for its ancient murals and spiritual significance. Later, visit Mebar Tsho, popularly known as the Burning Lake, one of Bhutan's most sacred pilgrimage sites and an excellent location for landscape and spiritual photography. Spend the evening exploring local markets and traditional settlements around Bumthang. Overnight at Bumthang.

itinerary.title: Bumthang (2,600m)
itinerary.meta: Transfer to Mongar (1,700m) · Approx. 200 km · Approx. 7–8 Hours
itinerary.desc: After breakfast, begin one of Bhutan's most scenic drives towards Eastern Bhutan. Enroute, visit Ura Valley, one of the most picturesque valleys in Bhutan, known for its traditional stone houses and peaceful rural landscapes. Continue the journey across Thrumshing La Pass (3,750m), the highest mountain pass on the Lateral East-West Highway, offering exceptional opportunities for mountain and landscape photography. As the road gradually descends, witness dramatic changes in vegetation and scenery before arriving in Mongar. If time permits, visit a traditional farmhouse in Sengor Village and experience authentic rural Bhutanese life. Overnight at Mongar.

itinerary.title: Mongar (1,700m)
itinerary.meta: Transfer to Trashiyangtse (1,850m) · Approx. 170 km · Approx. 6–7 Hours
itinerary.desc: After breakfast, drive further east through beautiful mountain landscapes and subtropical valleys. Pass through Lingmethang and other picturesque settlements while enjoying changing scenery and opportunities for documentary and landscape photography. Continue towards Trashiyangtse, one of Bhutan's least-visited regions, known for its peaceful environment, traditional craftsmanship and rich cultural heritage. Depending on arrival time, explore the town and surrounding landscapes. Overnight at Trashiyangtse.

itinerary.title: Trashiyangtse (1,850m)
itinerary.meta: Excursion & Transfer to Trashigang (1,150m) · Approx. 55 km · Approx. 2 Hours
itinerary.desc: This morning, visit the famous Gomphu Kora Monastery, one of Eastern Bhutan's most important pilgrimage sites associated with Guru Rinpoche. Continue to Chorten Kora, one of Bhutan's most significant stupas, where annual religious festivals attract devotees from Bhutan and neighbouring Arunachal Pradesh in India. Enjoy photography opportunities around the numerous prayer wheels, traditional villages and local communities. Later, drive towards Trashigang, the commercial and cultural centre of Eastern Bhutan. Overnight at Trashigang.

itinerary.title: Trashigang (1,150m)
itinerary.meta: Transfer to Samdrupjongkhar (250m) · Approx. 180 km · Approx. 6–7 Hours
itinerary.desc: After breakfast, begin your scenic descent towards Samdrupjongkhar. The journey offers excellent opportunities to photograph changing landscapes as you descend from the cool mountain regions into subtropical forests and lower valleys. Enroute, make several photography stops to capture rural life, traditional settlements and the diverse natural scenery of Eastern Bhutan. Arrive in Samdrupjongkhar by evening and enjoy your final night in Bhutan. Overnight at Samdrupjongkhar.

itinerary.title: Departure from Samdrupjongkhar
itinerary.desc: After breakfast, bid farewell to your Bhutanese hosts and conclude your memorable photography journey through the Kingdom of Bhutan. Depart with unforgettable memories and a remarkable collection of photographs capturing Bhutan's landscapes, culture, monasteries and unique way of life.

visa.title: Bhutan Visa & Entry Permit Guide
visa.html:
Bhutan visa and entry permit guide for Indian and International Travellers

Introduction

Planning a journey to Bhutan begins with understanding the correct visa or Entry Permit requirements for your nationality.

Indian nationals do not require a tourist visa for Bhutan. They must obtain an Entry Permit using an accepted Indian travel document. Travellers holding passports from most other countries must obtain an approved Bhutan tourist e-visa before entering the kingdom.

Bangladeshi and Maldivian nationals require a visa but may apply before travelling or complete the process on arrival, subject to immigration clearance.

La Bhutanz Tours assists travellers from India and around the world with personalised Bhutan tour planning, documentation guidance, visa or permit coordination, Sustainable Development Fee information and carefully arranged travel logistics.

This guide explains the current Bhutan tourist visa and Entry Permit requirements for travellers planning to visit Bhutan in 2026.

Quick Bhutan visa and entry permit guide

Indian Citizens

Indian citizens do not require a tourist visa. They require a Bhutan Entry Permit and must carry a valid Indian passport or Indian voter identity card.

Bangladesh and Maldives Citizens

Bangladeshi and Maldivian passport holders require a Bhutan visa. They may apply online before travelling or obtain a visa on arrival, subject to immigration approval.

Other International Travellers

Travellers holding passports from most other countries must obtain an approved Bhutan tourist e-visa before arriving in Bhutan.

NRI and OCI Travellers

The applicable process is determined by the passport used for travel. An Indian passport follows the Entry Permit process, while a foreign passport follows the visa rules applicable to that nationality.

Final Entry Decision

Possession of an approved visa or permit does not automatically guarantee admission. Final entry into Bhutan is determined by immigration officials at the port of entry.

Do Indian citizens need a visa for Bhutan?

No. Indian citizens do not require a tourist visa to visit Bhutan.

Indian nationals must obtain a Bhutan Entry Permit before travelling or at an authorised port of entry. The permit allows the traveller to enter and travel in Bhutan for the approved dates and itinerary.

Although Indian travellers can apply on arrival, arranging the permit before departure is recommended. Advance processing can reduce waiting time and allows identity details, travel dates and documentation to be checked before the journey begins.

Documents required for Indian adults travelling to Bhutan

Indian nationals aged 18 years and above should carry one of the following accepted travel documents:

  • A valid Indian passport; or
  • A valid voter identity card issued by the Election Commission of India

When travelling with a passport, it must have a minimum validity of six months from the intended date of departure from Bhutan.

Travellers should also prepare:

  • A recent passport-size photograph
  • Confirmed arrival and departure dates
  • Accommodation and itinerary details
  • Contact information
  • Sustainable Development Fee payment details
  • Any additional document requested during immigration assessment

The name, date of birth and identity-document number used for the permit must match the traveller’s original document exactly.

Aadhaar, PAN card and driving licence

Can indians travel to Bhutan using an aadhaar card?

Indian travellers should not rely on an Aadhaar card, PAN card or driving licence as their primary Bhutan entry document.

The officially accepted travel documents for Indian adults are:

  • A valid Indian passport
  • A valid Indian voter identity card

Travellers should carry the original accepted document used in the Entry Permit application throughout the journey.

Documents required for Indian children below 18 years

Indian nationals below the age of 18 may travel using:

  • A valid Indian passport; or
  • An original birth certificate

Minor travellers must be accompanied by a legal guardian.

Parents or guardians should also carry:

  • A recent passport-size photograph of the child
  • The child’s original birth certificate when a passport is unavailable
  • The passport or voter ID of the accompanying parent or guardian
  • Supporting proof of relationship where necessary
  • A consent letter when the child is travelling with only one parent or another guardian

All names and personal details should be consistent across the documents submitted.

How to apply for a Bhutan entry permit online

Indian travellers may apply for their Entry Permit online before travelling to Bhutan.

The application may be completed:

  • Directly by the traveller
  • By a tour operator on the traveller’s behalf
  • By a participating accommodation provider

The usual process includes:

1. Preparing the accepted identity document

2. Uploading a recent passport-size photograph

3. Providing the intended arrival and departure dates

4. Entering accommodation and travel information

5. Paying the applicable sustainable development fee

6. Submitting the permit application for assessment

7. Keeping a digital and printed copy of the approved permit

Travellers must carry the original passport or voter identity card used for the application when entering Bhutan.

Can Indian Travellers obtain a Bhutan permit on Arrival?

Yes. Indian nationals are eligible to request an Entry Permit at an authorised port of entry.

For an on-arrival permit, travellers should carry:

  • Original Indian passport or voter identity card
  • Recent passport-size photograph
  • Accommodation details
  • Travel itinerary
  • Arrival and departure information
  • Sustainable Development Fee payment arrangement

Permit-on-arrival processing may involve waiting, particularly during festivals, public holidays and peak travel periods.

Advance permit processing is therefore recommended for travellers seeking a smoother and more predictable arrival experience.

Bhutan entry permit for Indian Travellers arriving by Air

Indian travellers flying to Bhutan complete immigration formalities at Paro International Airport.

Travellers should keep the following documents readily accessible:

  • Original passport or voter identity card
  • Approved Entry Permit, when arranged in advance
  • Recent passport-size photograph
  • Flight details
  • Accommodation information
  • Return or onward travel details
  • Sustainable Development Fee payment confirmation

Immigration officials will verify the traveller’s documents and determine admission at the airport.

Bhutan entry permit for Indian Travellers arriving by road

Indian travellers entering Bhutan by road must complete immigration formalities at an authorised land port of entry.

Travellers commonly entering through Phuentsholing should ensure that their identity documents, travel dates, accommodation arrangements and onward itinerary are properly coordinated.

Before beginning the journey, confirm:

  • The authorised border entry point
  • Border and immigration operating arrangements
  • Original passport or voter identity card
  • Approved Entry Permit, when processed in advance
  • Hotel confirmations
  • Vehicle and driver details
  • Sustainable Development Fee payment
  • Planned travel dates and destinations

Old information stating that Indian travellers may initially visit only Paro and Thimphu should not be relied upon. The approved permit and itinerary should accurately reflect the traveller’s intended journey.

Immigration procedures and operational timings may change, so current arrangements should be reconfirmed before departure.

Bhutan sustainable development fee for Indian Travellers

Indian nationals presenting a valid Indian passport or voter identity card currently pay the following Sustainable Development Fee:

Adults and Travellers aged 12 years or above

Nu. 1,200 or the equivalent amount in Indian rupees per person, per night

Children aged 6 to below 12 years

Nu. 600 or INR 600 per child, per night

Children Below 6 Years

No sustainable development fee

The SDF is separate from:

  • Hotel accommodation
  • Meals
  • Private transport
  • Licensed guide services
  • Monument and attraction fees
  • Flights
  • Personal expenses
  • Travel insurance
  • Tour planning and operational services

The final SDF is calculated according to the traveller’s age, nationality and number of chargeable nights in Bhutan.

Bhutan visa for bangladeshi and maldivian Travellers

Citizens of Bangladesh and the Maldives require a visa to visit Bhutan.

They may:

  • Apply online before travelling; or
  • Apply for a visa on arrival at an authorised port of entry

Advance application is recommended to reduce waiting time and allow documentation to be checked before departure.

Travellers should normally prepare:

  • A valid passport
  • Recent passport-size photograph
  • Arrival and departure dates
  • Accommodation information
  • Travel itinerary
  • Sustainable Development Fee payment
  • Any additional document requested by immigration

The passport should have a minimum validity of six months from the intended date of departure from Bhutan.

Final visa approval and admission remain subject to assessment by Bhutanese immigration authorities.

Sustainable development fee for bangladesh and maldives citizens

Bangladeshi and Maldivian travellers are not eligible for the reduced Indian SDF rate.

The standard international Sustainable Development Fee applies:

Adults and Travellers aged 12 years or above

US$100 per person, per night

Children aged 6 to below 12 years

US$50 per child, per night

Children Below 6 Years

No sustainable development fee

The applicable visa-processing charge and payment instructions should be confirmed through the official immigration application system when the application is submitted.

Bhutan tourist visa for International Travellers

Most foreign nationals, other than Indian citizens and travellers covered by specific visa-on-arrival arrangements, must obtain an approved Bhutan tourist e-visa before entering the country.

Travellers should not arrive in Bhutan without receiving the required visa approval.

The tourist e-visa process applies to travellers from countries including:

  • United States
  • United Kingdom
  • Canada
  • Australia
  • New Zealand
  • European countries
  • Middle Eastern countries
  • African countries
  • East Asian and Southeast Asian countries
  • South American countries
  • Other international markets

Bhutan does not publish a general list of nationalities prohibited from applying for a tourist visa. However, every application remains subject to immigration assessment.

Approval of a visa does not remove the requirement to complete immigration formalities upon arrival.

Documents required for a Bhutan tourist e-visa

International travellers should prepare the following information and documents:

  • Clear digital copy of a valid passport
  • Recent digital passport-size photograph
  • Intended arrival date
  • Intended departure date
  • Accommodation details
  • Travel itinerary
  • Contact information
  • Payment details for the visa application fee and SDF
  • Any additional supporting document requested by immigration

Passport Validity

The passport must have a minimum validity of six months from the intended date of departure from Bhutan.

Document Accuracy

The traveller’s full name, date of birth, nationality, passport number and passport validity dates must be entered exactly as shown in the passport.

Incorrect or inconsistent information may delay assessment or require the application to be corrected and resubmitted.

How to apply for a Bhutan tourist visa

Step 1: confirm Your travel dates

Finalise the intended arrival and departure dates. These dates determine the requested visa period and the Sustainable Development Fee calculation.

Step 2: check Your passport

Ensure that the passport will remain valid for at least six months from the intended date of departure from Bhutan.

Step 3: prepare Your documents

Prepare a clear passport scan, recent passport photograph, accommodation details and travel information.

Step 4: Complete the Application

The traveller may apply directly through Bhutan’s official online immigration system. A tour operator or participating hotel may also submit the application on the traveller’s behalf.

Step 5: pay the required charges

Pay the applicable visa application fee and Sustainable Development Fee through the approved application process.

Step 6: Submit the Application

Review all personal and travel details carefully before submitting the application.

Step 7: Wait for Assessment

A correctly completed tourist visa application may take up to five working days to process.

Step 8: receive the approved e-visa

Keep a digital copy and printed copy of the visa approval.

Step 9: travel with the same passport

The traveller must enter Bhutan using the same passport used in the visa application.

Step 10: complete immigration formalities

Final admission is determined by immigration officials at the port of entry.

Bhutan tourist visa application fee

The standard Bhutan tourist visa application fee is:

US$40 per person

This is a one-time, non-refundable visa application fee.

The visa fee is separate from:

  • Sustainable Development Fee
  • Accommodation
  • Flights
  • Transport
  • Guide services
  • Meals
  • Attraction fees
  • Travel insurance
  • Tour arrangements

Travellers should verify the final amount shown in the official application portal before making payment.

Bhutan sustainable development fee for International Travellers

The current Sustainable Development Fee for most international visitors is:

Adults and Travellers aged 12 years or above

US$100 per person, per night

Children aged 6 to below 12 years

US$50 per child, per night

Children Below 6 Years

No sustainable development fee

The SDF is calculated according to the number of chargeable nights spent in Bhutan.

The SDF supports Bhutan’s national development, environmental conservation, cultural preservation, infrastructure, education, healthcare and initiatives that help protect the kingdom’s distinctive travel environment.

How long Does a Bhutan tourist visa take?

A correctly completed Bhutan tourist visa application may take up to five working days to process.

Travellers should apply well before their intended departure date because additional time may be required when:

  • Information is incomplete
  • Passport details are incorrect
  • Photographs or scans are unclear
  • Additional documents are requested
  • Payment confirmation is delayed
  • Public holidays affect processing
  • Travel dates or passport information change

International travellers should avoid confirming non-refundable travel arrangements until the required documentation and travel conditions have been carefully reviewed.

How long Can a tourist stay in Bhutan?

The Bhutan tourist visa allows an international traveller to remain in the country for a maximum of 90 days from the date of entry.

The approved visa dates, travel itinerary and Sustainable Development Fee payment should accurately reflect the intended stay.

Travellers planning to change or extend their journey should address the required visa, permit and SDF adjustments before altering their confirmed arrangements.

Approval of an extension is subject to the applicable immigration rules and official assessment.

Is travel insurance mandatory for Bhutan?

Bhutan’s Department of Tourism announced in April 2024 that the mandatory tourist travel-insurance requirement introduced during the COVID-19 period had been lifted.

However, some Department of Immigration information pages may still display travel insurance among the listed application requirements.

Travellers should therefore check the live application portal and current instructions at the time of applying.

Even when it is not mandatory, comprehensive travel insurance is strongly recommended. Suitable cover should ideally include:

  • Emergency medical treatment
  • Medical evacuation
  • Trip cancellation
  • Travel delays
  • Missed flight connections
  • Lost or delayed baggage
  • Trekking or adventure activities, when applicable
  • Weather-related disruption

Insurance conditions vary by provider, age, nationality and planned activities.

Bhutan visa rules for NRI and OCI Travellers

The traveller’s entry category is determined by the passport used for the Bhutan journey.

Travelling on an Indian Passport

The traveller follows the Indian Entry Permit process and may qualify for the Indian Sustainable Development Fee rate.

Travelling on a Foreign Passport

The traveller follows the Bhutan visa rules applicable to the nationality shown on that passport.

OCI Card Holders

An Overseas Citizen of India card does not replace the passport required for international travel and does not automatically qualify the traveller for the Indian Entry Permit or reduced Indian SDF rate.

Dual-Nationality Travellers

Travellers should use one passport consistently for:

  • Flight reservations
  • Visa or permit application
  • Hotel documentation
  • Immigration clearance
  • Entry into and departure from Bhutan

NRI, OCI and dual-nationality travellers should confirm the passport they will use before permit, visa, flight and SDF arrangements are finalised.

Visa, permit and SDF changes

Travellers should ensure that their approved visa or permit dates match the final travel itinerary.

Changes to the journey may require:

  • Updating travel dates
  • Revising accommodation information
  • Adjusting the visa or permit
  • Paying an additional Sustainable Development Fee
  • Requesting an SDF refund for a shortened or cancelled journey

The Sustainable Development Fee may be refundable for an eligible cancelled or shortened trip, after applicable bank charges.

The visa application fee is non-refundable.

Refund and amendment requests should be submitted through the official system and remain subject to the applicable government procedures.

Important Bhutan visa and permit guidance

Use only current official immigration requirements.

  • Do not rely on old information stating that Indian travellers are limited to Paro and Thimphu.
  • Carry the original passport, voter ID or birth certificate used for the application.
  • Ensure that all names, passport numbers and dates are entered correctly.
  • Keep digital and printed copies of the approved visa or permit.
  • Confirm that the approved travel dates match the final itinerary.
  • Apply in advance whenever possible to reduce arrival delays.
  • Do not treat a visa or permit as an automatic guarantee of entry.
  • Immigration officials may request additional documents.
  • Requirements, fees and procedures can change through government notification.
  • Reconfirm current rules before departure, especially when entering by road.

How La Bhutanz Tours assists with Bhutan visa and entry permit planning

La Bhutanz Tours supports Indian and international travellers with clear, practical guidance throughout the Bhutan travel-planning process.

Our assistance may include:

  • Identifying whether the traveller requires a visa or Entry Permit
  • Reviewing basic document readiness
  • Coordinating tourist visa or permit applications where applicable
  • Checking passport and identity-document details
  • Aligning application dates with the itinerary
  • Calculating the applicable Sustainable Development Fee
  • Coordinating accommodation and private transport
  • Planning fly-in and overland journeys
  • Sharing approved travel documents before departure
  • Assisting with changes when travel arrangements are revised
  • Providing destination and arrival guidance

Visa and Permit Approval

All visas and Entry Permits are issued by the relevant Bhutanese government authority.

La Bhutanz Tours cannot guarantee visa or permit approval, influence an immigration decision or override the requirements of Bhutan’s Department of Immigration.

Our role is to help travellers prepare carefully, understand the process and coordinate their Bhutan journey with greater clarity.

Frequently Asked Questions about Bhutan visas and entry permits

1. Do Indian citizens need a visa for Bhutan?

No. Indian citizens require a Bhutan Entry Permit rather than a tourist visa. They must use a valid Indian passport or voter identity card.

2. Can Indians apply for a Bhutan Entry Permit online?

Yes. Indian travellers may apply online before travelling. A tour operator or participating hotel may also apply on their behalf.

3. Can Indians obtain a Bhutan Permit on arrival?

Yes. Indian nationals are eligible for an Entry Permit at an authorised port of entry. Advance processing is recommended because on-arrival applications may involve waiting.

4. Can an Indian citizen enter Bhutan with an Aadhaar card?

Travellers should not rely on Aadhaar as the primary entry document. Indian adults should use a valid Indian passport or voter identity card.

5. What document does an Indian child need?

An Indian child below 18 may use a valid passport or original birth certificate and must travel with a legal guardian.

6. How much SDF do Indian citizens pay?

Indian travellers aged 12 and above pay Nu. 1,200 or the equivalent in Indian rupees per night. Children aged 6 to below 12 pay Nu./INR 600 per night, while children below 6 are exempt.

7. Do Bangladesh citizens need a Bhutan visa?

Yes. Bangladeshi passport holders require a visa but may apply before travelling or obtain it on arrival, subject to immigration approval.

8. Do Maldives citizens need a Bhutan visa?

Yes. Maldivian passport holders require a visa but may apply online in advance or obtain it on arrival.

9. Do American, British, Canadian, Australian and European travellers need a visa?

Yes. Travellers holding ordinary passports from these countries must normally obtain an approved Bhutan tourist e-visa before entering Bhutan.

10. How much is the Bhutan tourist visa fee?

The standard tourist visa application fee is US$40 per person. It is a one-time, non-refundable fee.

11. How much is the SDF for international travellers?

The standard SDF is US$100 per adult per night. Children aged 6 to below 12 pay US$50 per night, while children below 6 are exempt.

12. How long does a Bhutan visa application take?

A correctly completed application may take up to five working days. Applying earlier is advisable.

13. How long can a tourist stay in Bhutan?

A tourist visa allows a maximum stay of 90 days from the date of entry, subject to the approved arrangements.

14. Can a tour operator apply for the visa?

Yes. A tour operator or participating hotel may submit an application on behalf of the traveller when provided with the required information and documents.

15. Is travel insurance compulsory?

The mandatory tourist-insurance requirement was officially lifted in April 2024, but travellers should check the current application instructions. Comprehensive travel insurance remains strongly recommended.

16. Does an OCI card qualify for the Indian Entry Permit?

An OCI card alone does not replace a passport. The applicable process depends on the passport used for the journey.

17. Does an approved visa guarantee entry into Bhutan?

No. Final admission is determined by Bhutanese immigration officials at the port of entry.

18. Can La Bhutanz Tours guarantee visa approval?

No. We can assist with guidance and coordination, but only Bhutan’s authorised immigration authority can approve or refuse a visa or Entry Permit.

festivals.title: Bhutan Festivals & Tshechu
festivals.html:
Bhutan festivals and tshechu celebrations

Bhutan’s festivals offer travellers a meaningful opportunity to experience the Kingdom’s living Buddhist traditions, sacred masked dances, music, community gatherings and colourful national dress.

Known locally as tshechus, many of these celebrations are held annually at dzongs, monasteries and temples across Bhutan. They are not simply cultural performances for visitors; they are important religious and social occasions where Bhutanese communities gather to receive blessings, honour Guru Rinpoche and celebrate their shared heritage.

From the renowned Paro and Thimphu Tshechus to the sacred Jambay Lhakhang Drup in Bumthang and the community-led Black-Necked Crane Festival in Phobjikha Valley, each celebration reflects the history, spiritual traditions and regional identity of its destination.

Festival dates generally follow the Bhutanese lunar calendar and may change each year. Travellers should therefore confirm the official dates before arranging flights, accommodation or a festival-focused Bhutan journey.

Why festivals matter in Bhutan

Bhutan’s festivals are important religious and social occasions that bring communities together through prayer, sacred performances, traditional dress, music and shared celebration.

For local families, a tshechu is an opportunity to receive blessings, reconnect with relatives and participate in traditions passed down through generations.

For travellers, festivals offer a deeper understanding of Bhutanese culture. The experience goes beyond watching masked dances; it includes observing community life, spiritual rituals, traditional clothing and the atmosphere surrounding the dzong, monastery or village where the celebration takes place.

Each festival reflects the history and identity of its region. Some are large and well known, while others are smaller, more intimate and closely connected to local communities.

A meaningful festival journey should therefore allow enough time to experience the destination itself, not only the main performance.

Paro Tshechu

Paro Tshechu is one of Bhutan’s most celebrated religious festivals and is held annually at Rinpung Dzong in Paro.

The festival brings together monks, lay performers, local families and visitors for several days of sacred masked dances, traditional music, prayer and community celebration.

One of the most important moments is the unveiling of the giant thangka, known as the thongdrel, in the early morning on the final day. Bhutanese people believe that simply viewing the sacred image brings spiritual blessings.

Paro Tshechu is especially meaningful because it combines religious tradition with the atmosphere of Paro Valley, one of Bhutan’s most culturally significant destinations.

Travellers planning to attend should allow enough time to experience not only the festival, but also nearby places such as Rinpung Dzong, the National Museum, traditional villages and Tiger’s Nest Monastery.

Thimphu Tshechu

Thimphu Tshechu is one of Bhutan’s largest and most widely attended religious festivals. It is held at Tashichho Dzong in the capital city of Thimphu.

The festival features sacred masked dances, traditional music, colourful costumes and religious performances presented by monks and trained lay dancers.

For Bhutanese families, Thimphu Tshechu is an important occasion to receive blessings, wear national dress and gather with relatives and friends.

The festival also allows travellers to experience Bhutanese culture within the setting of the country’s capital, where traditional heritage and modern life exist side by side.

Visitors attending Thimphu Tshechu can combine the festival with cultural experiences such as Buddha Dordenma, Memorial Chorten, traditional craft centres, local markets and Tashichho Dzong.

Punakha Drubchen and Tshechu

Punakha Drubchen and Punakha Tshechu are among Bhutan’s most historically significant celebrations and are held at the magnificent Punakha Dzong.

Punakha Drubchen commemorates Bhutan’s seventeenth-century victory over Tibetan forces. The festival is known for its dramatic re-enactments, traditional warrior costumes and ceremonial performances that reflect an important chapter in Bhutanese history.

Punakha Tshechu follows the Drubchen and features sacred masked dances, religious rituals, traditional music and community gatherings.

The setting adds greatly to the experience. Punakha Dzong stands at the confluence of the Pho Chhu and Mo Chhu rivers and is considered one of Bhutan’s most beautiful architectural landmarks.

Travellers attending these celebrations can also explore the Punakha Suspension Bridge, Khamsum Yulley Namgyal Chorten, riverside villages and the warmer landscapes of Punakha Valley.

Jambay Lhakhang Drup

Jambay Lhakhang Drup is one of Bumthang’s most distinctive religious festivals and is held at the ancient Jambay Lhakhang in Chokhor Valley.

The festival is known for sacred masked dances, traditional rituals and community gatherings that continue over several days.

One of its best-known ceremonies is the Mewang, or fire blessing, in which participants pass beneath a burning arch as part of a purification ritual. Another important performance is the Tercham, a sacred dance associated with fertility and spiritual blessing.

The setting adds to the experience. Jambay Lhakhang is one of Bhutan’s oldest temples and forms part of Bumthang’s deeply spiritual landscape.

Travellers attending the festival can also explore Kurjey Lhakhang, Tamshing Lhakhang, Jakar Dzong, local villages and the wider Bumthang Valley.

Black-Necked Crane Festival

The Black-Necked Crane Festival is a community-led celebration held annually in Phobjikha Valley to welcome the arrival of the black-necked cranes at their winter roosting grounds.

Unlike Bhutan’s religious tshechus, this is a secular conservation festival. It helps raise awareness about the importance of protecting the cranes, their habitat and the wider ecosystem of Phobjikha Valley.

The programme commonly includes crane-themed dances performed by local schoolchildren, traditional songs, cultural performances, archery and community activities.

For travellers, the festival offers a meaningful combination of culture, conservation and nature. It is best experienced alongside visits to Gangtey Monastery, the Gangtey Nature Trail, local villages and crane-viewing areas across the valley.

Visitors should observe the birds quietly, avoid disturbing their habitat and follow local guidance when using cameras or binoculars.

Other important Bhutan festivals

Bhutan hosts many other regional festivals, each shaped by the traditions, history and landscape of its destination.

Some important celebrations include:

  • Gangtey Tshechu in Phobjikha Valley
  • Ura Yakchoe in Bumthang
  • Nimalung Tshechu in Bumthang
  • Kurjey Tshechu in Bumthang
  • Wangdue Tshechu in Wangdue Phodrang
  • Royal Highland Festival in Laya
  • Jakar Tshechu in Bumthang
  • Druk Wangyel Tshechu at Dochula
  • Trongsa Tshechu in central Bhutan
  • Chorten Kora Festival in Trashiyangtse

Smaller regional festivals can offer a more intimate atmosphere than the major celebrations in Paro and Thimphu. They may be especially suitable for travellers interested in photography, local communities, cultural immersion and less crowded experiences.

Festival dates and programmes can change, so travellers should always confirm the official annual calendar before finalising their journey.

How to plan a Bhutan festival Journey

A Bhutan festival journey requires careful planning because festival dates follow the lunar calendar and accommodation near major venues can be limited.

Begin by choosing the festival that best matches your interests. Paro and Thimphu Tshechus are ideal for first-time visitors who want to combine major cultural landmarks with a large celebration, while festivals in Bumthang, Phobjikha and eastern Bhutan may suit travellers seeking a quieter and more immersive experience.

Plan enough time around the festival rather than attending only for a few hours. A well-designed itinerary should include the destination’s monasteries, villages, landscapes and local experiences before or after the main event.

Consider the following while planning:

  • Confirm the official festival dates before booking flights
  • Reserve accommodation early for major festivals
  • Allow flexibility for programme changes and local ceremonies
  • Choose a private guide who can explain the dances and rituals
  • Carry suitable clothing for changing weather and long outdoor hours
  • Keep additional time for photography, local interaction and sightseeing

Festival journeys are most rewarding when they are planned at a comfortable pace and treated as a cultural experience rather than only a sightseeing stop.

Festival Etiquette in Bhutan

Bhutan’s festivals are sacred community occasions, so visitors should observe them with patience, respect and cultural sensitivity.

Dress modestly and comfortably. Clothing should cover the shoulders and knees, especially when the festival is held inside or near a dzong, monastery or temple.

Follow the instructions of your guide, monks and festival organisers. Some areas may be reserved for local participants, religious officials or ceremonial activities.

Ask permission before photographing monks, performers, children or local families. Photography may be restricted during certain rituals or inside religious spaces.

Avoid blocking pathways, standing directly in front of local participants or interrupting ceremonies for photographs.

Remain quiet during prayers, blessings and important religious performances. Mobile phones should be kept on silent.

Do not touch masks, costumes, religious objects or ceremonial items.

Festival grounds can become crowded, so carry only essential belongings, keep valuables secure and remain aware of local movement around you.

Most importantly, treat the festival as a living religious and cultural tradition rather than only as a performance for visitors.

Frequently Asked Questions about Bhutan festivals

When is the best time to attend a festival in Bhutan?

Festival dates vary each year because many follow the Bhutanese lunar calendar. Spring and autumn are especially popular, with major events such as Paro Tshechu, Thimphu Tshechu and several Bumthang festivals.

Do Bhutan festival dates change every year?

Yes. Most tshechus and religious festivals follow the lunar calendar, so the exact Gregorian dates can change from year to year. Travellers should confirm the official annual calendar before booking flights and hotels.

Which Bhutan festival is best for first-time visitors?

Paro Tshechu and Thimphu Tshechu are popular choices for first-time visitors because they can be combined easily with major sightseeing in western Bhutan.

Are Bhutan festivals religious or cultural events?

Many tshechus are primarily religious festivals, although they also include strong cultural and community elements. Some events, such as the Black-Necked Crane Festival, are secular community and conservation celebrations.

Can travellers photograph Bhutan festivals?

Photography is generally possible in outdoor festival areas, but visitors should follow local instructions, avoid blocking participants and ask permission before photographing monks, children or local families. Some rituals and indoor religious spaces may have restrictions.

What should travellers wear to a Bhutan festival?

Travellers should wear modest, comfortable clothing that covers the shoulders and knees. Layers are useful because festival days may involve long outdoor hours and changing temperatures.

How many days should be planned around a festival?

It is better to allow at least two or three days around the festival destination so there is enough time for the celebration, local sightseeing and possible programme changes.

Planning a festival journey requires accurate dates, locations and enough time around the celebration.

A Bhutan festival journey is most meaningful when the celebration is thoughtfully combined with the destination’s monasteries, valleys, villages and cultural experiences.

Whether you are interested in the renowned Paro or Thimphu Tshechu, the historic celebrations of Punakha, the sacred festivals of Bumthang or the Black-Necked Crane Festival in Phobjikha Valley, the itinerary should reflect your interests, preferred pace and travel dates.

Every traveller experiences Bhutan differently. If you'd like to understand which festival journey is the right fit for your travel style, we're always happy to share genuine guidance, answer your questions and help you plan a Bhutan journey that's thoughtfully curated around you.

about-bhutan.title: About Bhutan
about-bhutan.html:
About Bhutan – The Kingdom of the thunder dragon

Bhutan is a small Himalayan kingdom nestled between India and the Tibet Autonomous Region of China. Known locally as Druk Yul, meaning the “Land of the Thunder Dragon,” the country is admired for its dramatic mountain landscapes, ancient Buddhist heritage, traditional architecture and deeply rooted cultural values.

From the peaceful valleys of Paro, Thimphu and Punakha to the pristine landscapes of Gangtey and Bumthang, Bhutan offers travellers a rare opportunity to experience a country where cultural preservation, environmental responsibility and thoughtful development remain central to everyday life.

Bhutan is also widely associated with Gross National Happiness, a development philosophy introduced under the leadership of His Majesty the Fourth King Jigme Singye Wangchuck. The philosophy considers wellbeing, cultural preservation, environmental conservation and responsible governance alongside economic progress.

Often described as one of the world’s most peaceful and inspiring destinations, Bhutan continues to preserve its identity while welcoming travellers who value meaningful experiences, authentic cultural encounters and the natural beauty of the Eastern Himalayas.

Bhutan at a Glance

Official name: Kingdom of Bhutan

Local name: Druk yul – land of the thunder dragon

Location: Eastern Himalayas, between India and the Tibet autonomous region of china

Capital: Thimphu

Area: Approximately 38,394 square kilometres

Population: Approximately 790,000

Government: Democratic constitutional monarchy

Official Language: Dzongkha

Widely spoken language: english

Currency: Bhutanese Ngultrum (BTN)

Time zone: Bhutan time – UTC/GMT +6 hours

Religion: Vajrayana Buddhism is Bhutan’s spiritual and cultural foundation, while other religions are also practised

National Day: 17 December

National Dress: Gho for men and kira for women

National Sport: Archery

National Animal: Takin

National Bird: Raven

National flower: blue poppy

National tree: Himalayan cypress

Electricity: 230V, 50Hz; travellers may encounter Indian, British and European-style sockets

Where Is Bhutan located?

Bhutan is a landlocked country in the Eastern Himalayas, positioned between India to the south, east and west, and the Tibet Autonomous Region of China to the north.

Despite its relatively small size, Bhutan has remarkable geographical diversity. The country rises from subtropical lowlands in the south to forested valleys, high mountain passes and snow-covered Himalayan peaks in the north.

This varied landscape creates distinct climates, ecosystems and travel experiences across the country. Travellers can move from the warmer southern foothills around Phuentsholing to the temperate valleys of Thimphu, Punakha and Paro, before continuing towards the higher elevations of Gangtey, Bumthang and the northern Himalayan regions.

Bhutan’s mountainous terrain has also helped preserve its traditional communities, regional cultures, sacred sites and natural environment, making geography an important part of the country’s identity.

A Brief History of Bhutan

Bhutan’s history combines ancient settlement, Buddhist tradition, regional leadership and the gradual emergence of a unified Himalayan kingdom.

Archaeological discoveries indicate that people inhabited parts of Bhutan thousands of years ago. Before Buddhism became established, local communities followed indigenous spiritual traditions, including forms of Bon.

Buddhism began influencing Bhutan from around the seventh and eighth centuries. Guru Padmasambhava, also known as Guru Rinpoche, played an especially important role in the spread of Vajrayana Buddhism and is associated with many of Bhutan’s most sacred monasteries, temples and pilgrimage sites.

In the seventeenth century, Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal unified the country, strengthened its religious and administrative institutions and established the dual system of governance. Many of Bhutan’s great dzongs were built or expanded during this period and continue to serve as religious and administrative centres.

In 1907, Ugyen Wangchuck was elected Bhutan’s first hereditary king, establishing the Wangchuck dynasty. The monarchy guided Bhutan through a gradual process of modernisation while protecting the country’s cultural identity and independence.

Bhutan began opening carefully to the outside world during the twentieth century. The National Assembly was established in 1953, and the country later introduced planned development, modern education, healthcare and national infrastructure.

In 2008, Bhutan became a democratic constitutional monarchy under a written Constitution. The King remains Head of State, while elected governments are responsible for the country’s democratic administration.

Today, Bhutan continues to balance modern development with the preservation of its Buddhist heritage, natural environment and distinctive national identity.

Gross National Happiness

Bhutan is internationally known for Gross National Happiness, commonly referred to as GNH. This development philosophy was introduced by His Majesty the Fourth King Jigme Singye Wangchuck in the early 1970s.

Gross National Happiness reflects the belief that national progress should not be measured by economic growth alone. It also considers the physical, emotional, cultural, social and environmental wellbeing of the people.

The philosophy is commonly understood through four broad pillars:

  • Sustainable and equitable socio-economic development
  • Preservation and promotion of culture
  • Conservation of the natural environment
  • Good governance

These principles are further explored through areas such as health, education, psychological wellbeing, community vitality, living standards, cultural diversity, responsible use of time and ecological resilience.

For travellers, Gross National Happiness is not simply a slogan. Its influence can be seen in Bhutan’s approach to cultural preservation, environmental protection, community life, public services and carefully managed tourism.

Visitors should not expect every Bhutanese person to be constantly happy. Instead, GNH represents a long-term national commitment to creating conditions that support balanced and meaningful lives.

Bhutanese culture, language and people

Bhutan’s cultural identity is expressed through its architecture, clothing, language, religious traditions, festivals, arts and everyday community life.

Traditional Bhutanese architecture can be seen in dzongs, monasteries, temples, farmhouses and public buildings across the country. These structures are recognised for their painted woodwork, symbolic patterns, courtyards and distinctive forms, often created without the use of architectural plans in the conventional sense.

The national language is Dzongkha, meaning “the language of the dzong.” English is widely used in education, administration and tourism. Bhutan is also home to numerous regional languages and dialects, reflecting the cultural diversity of its valleys and communities.

Traditional dress remains an important part of Bhutanese identity. Men wear the gho, a knee-length robe secured with a woven belt, while women wear the kira, a long woven dress usually accompanied by a jacket called a tego.

Bhutanese society includes communities with different regional identities, languages and customs. Rather than viewing Bhutanese culture as uniform, travellers will notice variations in food, textiles, festivals, dialects and lifestyles as they move through western, central, eastern and southern Bhutan.

Hospitality, respect for elders, spiritual values and close community relationships remain important aspects of everyday life. Travellers are encouraged to approach local communities with curiosity and respect, particularly when visiting religious sites, rural villages and private homes.

Archery is Bhutan’s national sport and is often accompanied by singing, celebration and friendly competition. Traditional music, dance, weaving, woodcarving, painting and mask-making also continue to play an important role in Bhutanese cultural life.

Religion and Spiritual Heritage

Vajrayana Buddhism forms the spiritual and cultural foundation of Bhutan. Its influence can be seen in the country’s monasteries, temples, dzongs, festivals, architecture, art, daily rituals and community traditions.

The Drukpa Kagyu school is closely associated with Bhutan’s national identity, while the Nyingma tradition is also widely practised, particularly in eastern and central regions. Hinduism is practised by many communities in southern Bhutan, and the country’s Constitution protects freedom of religion.

Guru Padmasambhava, also known as Guru Rinpoche, holds a central place in Bhutanese spiritual history. He is believed to have introduced and strengthened Vajrayana Buddhism in the Himalayan region during the eighth century. Many sacred sites across Bhutan are connected with his life and teachings, including the iconic Tiger’s Nest Monastery in Paro.

Prayer flags, prayer wheels, stupas, mani walls and butter lamps are common features of Bhutan’s spiritual landscape. These are not merely decorative elements; they carry religious meaning and should be treated respectfully.

Visitors are welcome at many monasteries, temples and dzongs, although access may occasionally be restricted during ceremonies or religious events. Travellers should dress modestly, remove hats where required, avoid touching sacred objects and always ask before photographing monks, rituals or temple interiors.

Bhutan’s spiritual heritage is best approached with patience, sensitivity and genuine curiosity. For many travellers, quiet moments inside a monastery, conversations with monks or walks through sacred landscapes become some of the most meaningful experiences of the journey.

National Symbols of Bhutan

Bhutan’s national symbols reflect the Kingdom’s history, natural environment, spiritual traditions and cultural identity.

National Flag

The national flag is divided diagonally into yellow and orange sections. Yellow represents the authority and tradition of the monarchy, while orange symbolises Bhutan’s Buddhist spiritual heritage.

A white dragon, known as the Druk, appears across the centre of the flag. The dragon represents Bhutan as Druk Yul, the Land of the Thunder Dragon. Its white colour signifies purity, while the jewels held in its claws represent the wealth, security and wellbeing of the nation.

National Emblem

Bhutan’s national emblem includes a double diamond thunderbolt above a lotus, flanked by two dragons and surmounted by a jewel. The emblem symbolises the unity of spiritual and civil traditions, the purity of Buddhist teachings and the sovereignty of the Kingdom.

National Animal – Takin

The takin is a distinctive Himalayan mammal known for its unusual appearance and strong association with Bhutanese folklore. It can be seen at the Motithang Takin Preserve in Thimphu and in selected mountain regions.

National Bird – Raven

The raven is considered sacred in Bhutan and is associated with the protective deity Mahakala. A raven also appears on the crown of Bhutan’s monarchs.

National flower – blue poppy

The blue poppy is Bhutan’s national flower. It grows in high-altitude Himalayan regions and is admired for its delicate blue petals and ability to survive in challenging mountain environments.

National tree – Himalayan cypress

The Himalayan cypress is valued for its strength, resilience and religious importance. Cypress trees are commonly found near monasteries, temples and sacred sites.

National Sport – Archery

Archery is Bhutan’s national sport and an important social tradition. Matches are often lively occasions accompanied by singing, dancing, celebration and friendly rivalry.

National Dress

The gho is the traditional national dress for men, while women wear the kira, usually accompanied by a tego jacket. Traditional dress remains widely worn at schools, government offices, religious occasions and festivals.

National Day

Bhutan celebrates National Day on 17 December. The date commemorates the coronation of Ugyen Wangchuck as the country’s first hereditary king in 1907.

Nature, Forests and Wildlife

Bhutan is internationally recognised for its commitment to environmental conservation. More than 70 percent of the country remains under forest cover, while the Constitution requires Bhutan to maintain at least 60 percent forest cover for all time.

The country’s landscapes range from subtropical forests and river valleys in the south to temperate woodlands, alpine meadows and snow-covered Himalayan regions in the north. This wide variation in altitude creates rich ecosystems within a relatively small geographical area.

Bhutan’s protected areas include national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, nature reserves and biological corridors that allow wildlife to move between habitats. Together, these conservation areas protect a significant portion of the country.

Bhutan is home to diverse wildlife, including the takin, red panda, Himalayan black bear, clouded leopard, snow leopard, Bengal tiger, golden langur and several species of deer.

The country is also an important destination for birdlife. Black-necked cranes migrate to the Phobjikha and Bumdeling valleys during winter, while hornbills, Himalayan monals, ravens and numerous other species can be observed across different regions.

Travellers can experience Bhutan’s natural heritage through forest walks, birdwatching, wildlife excursions, river valleys, mountain passes and community-based nature experiences.

Visitors should avoid disturbing wildlife, removing plants, leaving litter or walking outside designated trails. Responsible behaviour helps protect Bhutan’s fragile ecosystems and supports the communities that depend on them.

Weather and Climate in Bhutan

Bhutan’s climate varies significantly according to altitude, location and season. Travellers may experience subtropical conditions in the southern foothills, temperate weather in the central valleys and much colder alpine conditions in the higher Himalayan regions.

Spring – March to May

Spring generally brings pleasant temperatures, flowering trees, rhododendrons and increasingly green landscapes. It is a popular season for cultural sightseeing, photography, nature walks and trekking.

Summer and monsoon – june to September

Summer is warmer and greener, with rainfall influenced by the Indian monsoon. Rain is generally heavier in the southern regions, while central valleys often experience showers followed by clearer periods. Travellers should expect occasional road delays and carry suitable rain protection.

Autumn – late September to November

Autumn usually offers clear skies, comfortable daytime temperatures and excellent visibility of the Himalayan ranges. It is also an important season for festivals, trekking and cultural journeys.

Winter – December to February

Winter is generally dry, crisp and sunny, although mornings and evenings can be cold. Snowfall is possible at higher elevations and mountain passes, while valleys such as Punakha and Phuentsholing remain comparatively warmer.

Because weather can change quickly in mountainous regions, travellers should carry layers throughout the year. Conditions may differ significantly between Paro, Thimphu, Punakha, Gangtey and Bumthang during the same journey.

Festivals and Traditional Celebrations

Bhutan’s festivals are among the most meaningful ways to experience the country’s living culture, spiritual traditions and community life.

The best-known celebrations are tshechus, annual religious festivals held in different districts, monasteries and dzongs across Bhutan. The word tshechu refers to the tenth day of a month in the Bhutanese lunar calendar, traditionally associated with Guru Rinpoche.

Tshechus usually feature sacred masked dances, traditional music, religious ceremonies, colourful costumes and community gatherings. For Bhutanese families, these festivals are occasions to receive blessings, reconnect with relatives and celebrate their shared cultural heritage.

Some of Bhutan’s best-known festivals include:

  • Paro Tshechu
  • Thimphu Tshechu
  • Punakha Drubchen and Tshechu
  • Trongsa Tshechu
  • Jambay Lhakhang Drup in Bumthang
  • Black-Necked Crane Festival in Phobjikha Valley
  • Royal Highland Festival in Laya

Festival dates are generally determined according to the Bhutanese lunar calendar and may change from year to year. Travellers should therefore confirm the official dates before arranging flights, accommodation or a festival-focused itinerary.

Visitors should dress respectfully, avoid blocking local participants, ask permission before photographing people and follow any instructions given by monks, guides or festival organisers.

A Bhutan festival journey is most rewarding when there is enough time to experience the destination beyond the main performance, including its monasteries, villages, landscapes and local communities.

Currency and Payments in Bhutan

The official currency of Bhutan is the Bhutanese Ngultrum, abbreviated as BTN or written locally as Nu.

The Ngultrum is maintained at equal value with the Indian Rupee. Indian Rupees are widely accepted in Bhutan, although travellers should carry a practical combination of local currency, Indian Rupees and payment cards rather than relying on a single payment method.

Currency can be exchanged at Paro International Airport, authorised exchange counters, banks and selected larger hotels.

Visa and Mastercard are accepted at many hotels, restaurants and shops in major towns such as Paro and Thimphu. However, card acceptance may be limited in smaller towns, rural areas and local markets.

ATMs are available in major towns, but international cards may not work consistently. Travellers should inform their bank before departure, activate international transactions and check withdrawal limits.

Digital payment services are increasingly available in Bhutan, but visitors should still carry sufficient cash for small purchases, tips, rural stops and unexpected payment issues.

Exchange rates and payment arrangements can change. Travellers should confirm current banking and currency guidance before beginning their journey.

What to Pack for Bhutan

Packing for Bhutan depends on the season, altitude and regions included in your itinerary. Because temperatures can change considerably between daytime and evening, layered clothing is useful throughout the year.

Recommended clothing and essentials include:

  • Comfortable walking shoes with good grip
  • Lightweight clothing for warmer daytime conditions
  • A warm jacket, fleece or jumper for mornings and evenings
  • Waterproof or wind-resistant outerwear
  • Modest clothing for monasteries, temples and dzongs
  • Sunglasses, sunscreen and a reusable water bottle
  • Hat, gloves and thermal layers for winter or high-altitude journeys
  • Personal medication and a small basic travel kit
  • Rain protection during the summer and monsoon season
  • A universal travel adapter and portable power bank

Travellers visiting religious sites should wear clothing that covers the shoulders and knees. Comfortable trousers, long skirts and layered tops are generally practical for both sightseeing and cultural visits.

Those travelling to higher places such as Chele La, Dochula, Gangtey or Bumthang should carry additional warm layers even during otherwise pleasant seasons.

Avoid overpacking. Bhutan journeys often involve changing hotels and travelling through mountain roads, so manageable luggage is more convenient.
